mcqs.question: Why is a repeated lookup for a nonexistent key more dangerous than a normal cache miss on a real key?
options: It isn't more dangerous — both cost exactly the same over time
Nonexistent keys are automatically rate-limited by the database
It only matters if the key happens to be numeric
A normal cache miss is fixed after the value is cached once, but a nonexistent key never gets cached, so every request for it pays the full database cost forever
mcqs.explanation: A real key's miss is a one-time cost — after that first fetch, the cache holds it. A nonexistent key never gets a cache entry the same way, so identical repeated requests keep paying the full database round trip indefinitely, which is exactly what makes it exploitable at scale. Databases don't auto-rate-limit this, and key type (numeric or not) is irrelevant to the mechanism.

mcqs.question: What does negative caching actually store, and why does it use a short TTL?
options: It stores a marker that the key doesn't exist, with a short TTL so a later-created record still becomes visible reasonably quickly
It stores the last valid value the key ever had, refreshed rarely
It stores nothing — it simply blocks all future requests for that key
It uses a long TTL to permanently prevent ever checking that key again
mcqs.explanation: Negative caching stores a small "not found" sentinel for the key, and deliberately uses a short TTL so that if the record is created shortly after, users aren't stuck seeing "not found" for too long. It doesn't store an old valid value (there wasn't one), doesn't block future requests outright, and a long TTL would make newly-created records invisible for too long.

mcqs.question: How does probabilistic early expiration reduce the risk of many cache entries expiring and being recomputed at the exact same moment?
options: It disables TTLs entirely so nothing ever expires
It deletes entries early at random, regardless of their actual TTL
As an entry nears expiry, each request has a small, growing chance of triggering an early background recompute, spreading refreshes out over time
It only works for negative-cached entries, not regular ones
mcqs.explanation: The technique spreads out *when* recomputation happens by giving requests a rising probability of an early refresh as expiry approaches, rather than every request waiting for the same hard deadline. It doesn't disable TTLs or delete entries arbitrarily early without cause, and it applies to TTL-based caching generally, not only negative caching.

mcqs.question: A system is seeing high-volume, adversarial-looking requests for randomized, mostly nonexistent IDs. What's the better first line of defense, ahead of the cache itself?
options: Increase the negative-cache TTL to several hours
Remove negative caching, since it isn't helping against this traffic
A Bloom filter checked before the cache, to instantly reject keys that were never valid
Route all such requests directly to the database for a definitive answer
mcqs.explanation: A Bloom filter can reject a large share of never-valid keys before the cache (or database) is even consulted, which is exactly suited to high-volume, adversarial random-key traffic. Extending the negative-cache TTL doesn't address the adversarial volume itself, removing negative caching would make things worse, and routing straight to the database is the exact outcome being defended against.

mcqs.question: A database briefly times out while looking up a record that actually exists. The system negative-caches this as "not found" for 5 minutes. What's the consequence?
options: None — a timeout and a real "not found" are functionally identical and safe to treat the same
The database will automatically retry and overwrite the negative-cache entry
Only the original requester is affected, not other users
For the next 5 minutes, every legitimate request for that existing record incorrectly gets told it doesn't exist
mcqs.explanation: Negative-caching a transient error as a real absence means every subsequent request for that key — from any user — gets a false "not found" until the TTL expires, turning a brief blip into a self-inflicted outage. There's no automatic overwrite from a retry, the effect isn't limited to the original requester, and a timeout is meaningfully different from a confirmed absence — treating them the same is exactly the bug.

mcqs.question: A team doubles their Bloom filter's bits-per-element from 10 to 20 to cut the false-positive rate from about 1% to 0.01%. What did they trade for that improvement?
options: Roughly double the memory footprint of the filter
The ability to remove keys from the filter, which 10-bit filters could do
Slower lookup time proportional to the false-positive rate
Nothing — accuracy improves with no cost once you cross 10 bits per element
mcqs.explanation: Bits-per-element is a direct memory-vs-accuracy dial — doubling it roughly doubles memory use in exchange for a much lower false-positive rate. Removing keys isn't possible at either bit width without a full rebuild, and lookup time isn't the axis this tradeoff moves.
